title: North Carolina: a registered mark does not settle every business-opportunity trigger
description: Check the promise, the U.S. mark and the communication plan before deciding whether a filing branch applies.

sections.heading: Review each definition limb
paragraphs: North Carolina Article 19 covers specified arrangements for starting a business, tied to placement of vending machines or similar devices, purchases of products made by the buyer, income/refund promises, or a sales/marketing programme. Its federally registered-mark exception is in the marketing-programme limb of §66-94(4). It does not erase the other listed representations. A foreign registration or pending application should not be substituted for the stated U.S. registration condition.

sections.heading: Filing is separate from delivery to the purchaser
paragraphs: For a covered business opportunity, §66-97 requires filing before advertising or other representations to prospective purchasers in the state. The responsible-seller exemption in §66-94.1 has its own conditions and sworn filing; a company’s good reputation does not establish those conditions.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a cleaning-account programme

The guarantee needs its own analysis; account assistance does not by itself establish the separate vending-device placement trigger. Finance should assess any related bond or trust requirement.

sections.heading: Build two delivery calendars
paragraphs: Section 66-95 requires the covered state disclosure at least 48 hours before the earlier signature or receipt of consideration. It allows a materially compliant federal FDD as one content route. That does not shorten any independently applicable federal 14-calendar-day requirement. Retain the actual versions, delivery evidence and earliest commitment dates.

sections.heading: If the exemption is not established

The basic disclosure period is ten business days before agreement; Ohio defines business day by excluding Sunday and legal holidays. Do not silently use a Monday–Friday counter. Cancellation under §1334.05 is a separate conditional process, not a universal franchise cancellation right.

title: New Hampshire: distinguish operator support from a recruitment chain

sections.heading: Do not classify by the master label

The board should ask whether the economic engine is service to customers or successive participation payments, then document the complete facts for the statutory review. This scenario does not decide that a particular arrangement is unlawful.

sections.heading: Prepare the compensation-and-delivery map
bullets: Show every required upfront and continuing payment and its recipient.
Identify which participants receive recruiting rights and what conditions apply.
Separate customer-contract income from participant-recruitment income.
Cost actual training, field support and quality duties at each level.
Review the full scheme before offers; do not rely on a territory cap as an exemption.

sections.heading: Coverage is intentionally narrow
paragraphs: This chapter is not a complete franchise filing, disclosure or relationship-law survey. Federal franchise disclosure, New Hampshire consumer-protection law and industry dealer rules remain independent workstreams. An unknown filing column is not a finding that nothing applies.

practicalOutput: A recruitment compensation map with a named scheme-review task.
limitations: This page researches the named issue; it is not a complete state franchise or operating-law survey.
Federal disclosure and any independent state sales, relationship, sector and local duties must be checked for actual parties, places and activities.

title: New Hampshire: an industrial-equipment partner needs a dealer-law screen
description: The title of the motor-vehicle chapter does not tell you whether an equipment or authorised-service arrangement is covered.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Read the definition beyond the chapter title
paragraphs: RSA 357-C includes specified farm, utility, forestry, industrial, construction, yard and garden equipment within its defined framework. The actual seller and service arrangements matter. The chapter also defines certain service rights and identifies exceptions, including a specified single-line equipment dealer category.

sections.heading: Keep sales and service rights separate
paragraphs: The COO should record who can sell the equipment, who performs authorised service, whose trademarks are used and whether the business relies on continuing parts or supply. A service-only agreement for fleet, government or rental vehicles has express treatment in the definitions; do not assume every repair arrangement is the same.

sections.heading: Fictional example: an industrial maintenance brand
paragraphs: A European maintenance business wants its first operator to sell one equipment line and perform the manufacturer’s authorised warranty work. The team should test whether the state dealer chapter applies before relying solely on a generic service license. Its training and spare-parts commitments may also create costs absent from the service-only model.

sections.heading: Plan the relationship before the exit
paragraphs: The chapter contains good-faith, good-cause, notice and protest provisions for covered relationships. The complete 357-C:7 route must be reviewed for the event in question; this guide does not supply a universal notice period or determine an operator’s right to compensation.

sections.heading: Prepare a dealer-scope worksheet
bullets: Equipment and component descriptions, with actual uses.
Sales, distribution, service and warranty rights by entity.
Inventory-supplier concentration and any statutory single-line exception facts.
Customer types and any fleet/government/rental service limitation.
Proposed changes, termination grounds and source-backed review task.

practicalOutput: A product-and-service-specific dealer-law applicability worksheet.
limitations: This page researches the named issue; it is not a complete state franchise or operating-law survey.
Federal disclosure and any independent state sales, relationship, sector and local duties must be checked for actual parties, places and activities.

title: Nevada: do not copy farm-equipment dealer rules into every franchise
description: A product-and-parts arrangement may create a relationship workstream beyond the brand agreement.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: Start with the defined inventory and agreement
paragraphs: Nevada NRS 597.112–597.118 covers defined farm-equipment dealer relationships. It identifies retail inventory rights, a distribution-system role and substantial dependence on a supplier. Its inventory definition is farm equipment and attachments or repair parts; it is not a general definition covering every maintenance service or software license.

sections.heading: The exit requires more than a contract date
paragraphs: Section 597.1143 addresses good cause and generally requires 180 days written reasons before termination/nonrenewal, with 60 days to correct specified deficiencies. Several listed grounds are treated differently, and market-share failures have an assistance condition. A company should not assume that a broadly drafted contractual termination right answers these statutory questions.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a European equipment business
paragraphs: A manufacturer plans a Nevada operator that sells agricultural machines, holds parts and supplies branded servicing. Finance and operations should separately model inventory exposure, warranty responsibilities and continuing parts access. That work differs from licensing a pure consulting service.

sections.heading: Keep return values conditional
paragraphs: The chapter has repurchase rules and exclusions involving inventory condition, age and other facts, as well as specified supplier-required systems and tools. The company should retain evidence instead of assuming every inventory or technology cost will be reimbursed. Statutory nonwaiver provisions also deserve review.

sections.heading: Prepare the relationship file
bullets: List actual equipment, parts, suppliers and dealer rights.
Record inventory purchase dates, condition, catalogue status and invoices.
Document required systems, tools, warranty work and payment evidence.
Preserve performance notices, support offered and any proposed cure.
Assign sector-specific review; leave general franchise sales/filing coverage open until researched.

practicalOutput: A farm-equipment dealer-scope decision and inventory/exit evidence checklist.
limitations: This page researches the named issue; it is not a complete state franchise or operating-law survey.
Federal disclosure and any independent state sales, relationship, sector and local duties must be checked for actual parties, places and activities.

title: New Jersey: a B2B office or warehouse needs a franchise-relationship screen
description: The place-of-business inquiry has a B2B branch; calling the arrangement distribution does not finish it.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: A retail-shop assumption can miss the B2B facts
paragraphs: The enacted amendment to New Jersey’s Franchise Practices Act expressly addresses businesses that do not make a majority of sales directly to consumers. Its place-of-business wording includes qualifying offices or warehouses from which personnel visit or call customers or goods are delivered. This is a reason to investigate the actual operation, not a conclusion that every warehouse qualifies.

sections.heading: The wider relationship still matters
paragraphs: The Act’s definition addresses a written arrangement, licensed brand characteristics and a community of interest. A 2025 federal district-court opinion discusses why a self-described distribution label does not resolve those facts. That opinion was testing pleaded allegations, not making final findings of fact; it is used here for a bounded preparation lesson.

sections.heading: Fictional example: a technical-service network
paragraphs: A Dutch equipment-support business appoints an operator whose staff call on industrial customers from a New Jersey office. Before granting or withdrawing branded rights, the team records the sales process, office use, customer-facing identity and investment tied to the brand. A generic note saying no retail outlet is not sufficient evidence of nonapplication.

sections.heading: Prepare a separate state-law fact pack
bullets: What is sold, where it is offered and how customers interact with the operator.
Whether most sales go directly to consumers or to business buyers.
Brand rights, course of dealing and investment useful mainly within the relationship.
Actual place-of-business facts and sales/application criteria for review.
The current statute version, any industry rules and a named reviewer before a relationship action.

sections.heading: What remains unresolved
paragraphs: The current legislature LIS codification endpoint returned an error during review. The enacted amendment and the cited 2025 primary opinion were read, but this page does not certify the complete 2026 Act or decide a relationship’s legal status. Registration, notice, disclosure and advertising requirements remain separate research questions.

practicalOutput: A B2B location-and-relationship factsheet with an explicit current-codification review dependency.
limitations: Current full New Jersey codification could not be retrieved; publication is limited to the identified enacted amendment and primary judicial explanation.
No definitive 2026 eligibility, filing or termination conclusion is made.

title: New Mexico: verify enactment before using a termination template
description: The 2026 Franchise Termination Changes proposal died; its proposed deadlines cannot supply today’s checklist.
reviewStatus: AI-assisted primary-source review; no professional legal review

sections.heading: A published bill is not an operating rule
paragraphs: New Mexico’s official 2026 SB 115 status page lists the proposal as Died (API), with action postponed indefinitely. The introduced document and its analysis discuss expanded equipment definitions and termination protections, but those proposals did not become law through that bill.

sections.heading: Keep the proposed deadline out of the launch plan
paragraphs: A legislative analysis can describe when a measure would take effect if enacted. That conditional date is not proof that enactment occurred. The 2026 Fiscal Impact Report also says similar 2023 and 2025 proposals were not enacted. A copied notice period from one of those texts would give management an unsupported release condition.

sections.heading: Fictional example: an equipment-service supplier
paragraphs: A European machinery business finds a 2026 bill online and adds its proposed supplier-notice period to a U.S. dealer template. The corrected task is to identify the currently enacted statute, its equipment/dealer scope, the actual agreement and any applicable federal rule before issuing a notice. No current notice period is inferred from the failed proposal.

sections.heading: Create an enactment-and-applicability record
bullets: Save the exact bill, version, session and official final status.
Separate introduced text, legislative analysis, enacted chapter and current codification.
Record the actual products, dealer rights, parties and planned relationship action.
Assign retrieval and review of the current Franchise Termination Act before relying on a template.
Keep registration, disclosure, other dealer laws and local operating requirements as independent open workstreams.

sections.heading: Coverage limit
paragraphs: This guide verifies a high-consequence source-status distinction. It does not represent that the current codified Act was retrieved or that general franchise sales requirements are absent. The legal matrix leaves those questions unresolved instead of translating source gaps into permission to proceed.

practicalOutput: A bill-status audit and a task to obtain the applicable enacted relationship rules.
limitations: Current statutory coverage remains unresolved; the guide establishes the cited proposal’s non-enactment only.
No conclusion is made about general franchise filings, existing dealer protections or any termination’s validity.
